title: Validity, soundness, strength and cogency
note: A deductive argument is valid when it is impossible for its premises to be true and its conclusion false; it is sound when it is valid and its premises are true. An inductive argument is strong when true premises would make the conclusion probable, and cogent when it is strong with true premises. Validity is about form, so a counterexample with the same form can show invalidity.

read.title: Two questions for every argument
text: Every argument can be judged by asking two separate questions. First, do the premises support the conclusion? Second, are the premises true? Keeping these apart is one of the most useful habits in logic.

For deductive arguments, the first question is about validity. An argument is valid when there is no possible way for the premises to be true and the conclusion false. 'All cats can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly' is valid, because if the premises were true the conclusion would have to be. It is not sound, though, because its first premise is false. A sound argument is valid and has true premises, so its conclusion must be true.

Because validity depends on form, you can show an argument is invalid with a counterexample: an argument of exactly the same form with plainly true premises and a plainly false conclusion. 'All fish swim; Tom swims; so Tom is a fish' fails this way, since a dog can swim.

For inductive arguments, the first question is about strength, which comes in degrees. A strong argument whose premises are true is called cogent. Even a cogent argument can have a false conclusion; it only makes the conclusion likely.
